findings.title: Suppression allowlists cannot ratchet downward

evidence.note: The documented path-glob/rule format contains eleven active permission rows.
The consumer only asks whether an observed broad directive matches any permission; it does not record whether each permission was exercised.
The documented path-glob format grants two files permission to use file-level @ts-nocheck.
This consumer likewise implements only forward membership from an observed directive to an allowlist pattern.

evidence.measurement: At the audit pin, 11 of 11 non-comment ESLint allowlist rows correspond to at least one live broad directive, but 0 of 2 non-comment @ts-nocheck rows correspond to a real @ts-nocheck directive; both listed files still exist.
evidence.note: The TypeScript allowlist has already retained two unused grants, demonstrating that permissions survive suppression retirement.

findings.problem: Both registers reject newly observed suppressions outside their allowlists but never reject an allowlist row after its suppression disappears. The entirely stale @ts-nocheck list therefore remains a standing permission to reintroduce file-wide checking suppression in either named file without requiring a new policy exception, and the data inventory no longer describes current debt.
findings.proposedDirection: During full scans, track which allowlist rows match live directives and fail on unused rows, while preserving the existing independent source scan and glob formats. Limit stale-row validation to full-scan scope so changed-file scans do not infer repository-wide absence.

priorPackOverlap.novelty: CQ25-106 establishes independent discovery and non-vacuous scanning as a standing principle; these two allowlists and the measured 0-of-2 stale @ts-nocheck grants are new paths and evidence.
